title: The normalized integer difference is invariant under a common shift
statement: For all naturals m, n and k, the normalized difference of m+k and n+k is the normalized difference of m and n.

formal.statement: theorem Int.subNatNat_add_add : ((x0 : AxNat) -> ((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : AxNat) -> Eq.{1} Int (Int.subNatNat (AxNat.add x0 x2) (AxNat.add x1 x2)) (Int.subNatNat x0 x1))))

notes: The keystone lemma of this lane, and the smallest true statement about `Int.subNatNat` that is provable when its arguments are opaque. `subNatNat m n` is `Nat.rec ... (Nat.sub n m)` with `Nat.sub m n` in the zero minor; on variables neither subtraction reduces, so the term is stuck and the only thing it still respects is a common shift. The proof is induction on `k` -- `Nat.add` recurses on its second argument, so `m+(k+1)` is definitionally `(m+k)+1` and the step is the one-shot `subNatNat (m+1) (n+1) = subNatNat m n`, which is `Nat.succ_sub_succ` applied twice: once to the value and once to the scrutinee, since they sit in different holes and no single one-hole context covers both. Shifting the two anchors `subNatNat m 0 = ofNat m` and `subNatNat 0 k = negOfNat k` by this lemma is what yields the characterisations the whole rest of the development runs on. `formal.statement` is `Kernel::render_lean` of the admitted type, verbatim from `int_theorem_inventory`; `AxNat` is the renderer's emit-direction guard so that exporting our prelude does not shadow Lean's builtin `Nat`.
